sections.heading: 07 — Plain English Glossary
sections.intro:
Every technical term introduced across this knowledge package, defined the way the source material
defines it. Terms are alphabetical.

---

subsections.body:
**Constraints-led approach** — using an object, template, or step-by-step breakdown ("scaffolding")
to shape how a student solves a movement problem, rather than the object being the point of the
exercise.
subsections.heading: C

subsections.body:
**Differential learning** — deliberately varying a movement slightly on each repetition (e.g.
moving a hand's position) to expose a learner to more variation rather than one fixed pattern.
subsections.heading: D

subsections.body:
**Emulation** — the term used for the peer-engagement effect of training natural movement in a
large group rather than alone.
subsections.heading: E

subsections.body:
**Natural method** — the roughly hundred-year-old French physical education tradition based on
Georges Hébert's work, distinct from and older than MovNat.
subsections.heading: N

subsections.body:
**Points of support** — the parts of the body in contact with the ground or another surface at a
given moment; how these change as the body moves between positions is used to teach body
awareness.
subsections.heading: P

subsections.body:
- **Video ID:** `ljw0HURuuLM`
- **URL:** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ljw0HURuuLM
- **Upload date:** 2026-05-06
- **Duration:** 37:14
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/ljw0HURuuLM.txt`
- **Main subjects:** the get-up (demonstrated via the Turkish get-up pattern) taught live to two students, used to explain MovNat's broader teaching philosophy around constraints, tools, and the purpose of training, a stated distinction between "exercise" (mindless repetition) and "practicing movement" (purposeful, problem-solving)
- **Movements & practices:** the full get-up sequence — body-weight shift onto the bent leg, transfer to elbow, transfer to hand, half-kneeling transition, and standing — taught step by step to two students, use of a kettlebell held overhead as a constraint to teach smoother, more efficient movement through the same get-up pattern, use of a 100 lb sandbag to add load and demonstrate that loading through the hip/skeleton (rather than the tissue) makes the same movement dramatically easier
- **Evolutionary principles:** "the tool does not dictate the technique. The tool assists in the learning of the technique" — tools and added load are framed as teaching constraints, not the source of adaptation, a coach should always calibrate to "the lowest level of competency" of the student being taught, movement is classified into four domains: manipulative (moving objects/oneself relative to the environment), locomotive (getting from point A to point B), combative (striking and grappling), and expressive (moving for its own sake) — with get-up patterns identified as fundamentally combative movements with broader application
- **Important concepts:** points of support (the body parts in contact with a surface) and how they interact with the surface of support, reducing in number and stability from lying down to standing, tension versus relaxation as a trainable skill, distinct from raw strength, "differential learning" — varying a movement slightly on each repetition to gain more exposure to it, rather than repeating it identically, effectiveness (can the task be completed at all) versus efficiency (how well it is completed) as two separate axes for judging a movement attempt

subsections.body:
- **Video ID:** `NlQE1zMJwns`
- **URL:** https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NlQE1zMJwns
- **Upload date:** 2026-06-09
- **Duration:** 19:26
- **Source file:** `sources/clean/NlQE1zMJwns.txt`
- **Main subjects:** an interview with Gaspard Nouaille, a natural-method instructor in France, on his path from conventional sport and physical education into the "natural method" and then MovNat, the origins of the "natural method" in Georges Hébert's roughly 100-year-old French physical education tradition, and how MovNat adapted it for modern audiences
- **Movements & practices:** ground get-ups and floor-position exercises, singled out as the strongest addition MovNat gave the natural method, especially for city-dwelling adults "not used to get up and sit down anymore", throwing and balancing, named as the instructor's two favorite "families" of natural movement to teach, described as underestimated for what they develop
- **Evolutionary principles:** a stated cultural resistance to natural movement (crawling, hand-swings on a fixed object) because it looks "odd" next to conventional fitness norms, conventional functional fitness is described as disassociated from the actual purpose of a movement — e.g. deadlifting framed as "to get stronger" rather than "to carry something from point A to point B", the natural method's deliberate use of storytelling and imagination in group training to create emotional engagement, getting people to attempt movements ("climb into a tree because something is going on") they did not believe they could do
- **Important concepts:** balance described as revealing internal distraction, not just physical instability — losing balance is tied to "the life obstacles that are in their mind" intruding, group training "emulation" (peer engagement/mild peer pressure) named as a stated mechanism for why natural movement training works better in a large group than alone

sections.body:
**Gaspard Nouaille describes discovering the "natural method" of physical education — after a
childhood and youth built entirely around conventional sport (tennis, running, football, rugby,
etc.) — as "a revelation," and frames its value over conventional sport/fitness training as
reconnecting movement to a real purpose, taught through storytelling and group engagement rather
than isolated repetitions.** `[02:01]` "It's been quite a revelation for me because I didn't know
that natural movement at all at that time. I only did sports, and well, it's quite different,
actually."
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[01:00]`–`[02:01]` Gaspard's background is "a background of conventional sport" (tennis, climbing,
running, athleticism, handball, football, rugby, volleyball). In 2020, running physical education
at a Montessori school in France, he found conventional sport "not enough" and sought out a family
teaching Georges Hébert's natural method — a different lineage from Hébert's own descendants,
per the transcript. `[04:03]` He later discovered MovNat in 2023 at a Biarritz training and
completed a Level 3 training in Vienna in 2024, describing MovNat as adding "a lot of really
interesting tools and skills" to adapt the roughly hundred-year-old natural method "to the actual
needs" of modern people.
sections.heading: From conventional sport to the natural method to MovNat

sections.body:
`[08:06]`–`[09:08]` Asked about cultural resistance to natural movement, Gaspard says it can seem
"a bit odd" because "it's not in our culture." The interviewer extends this with his own
experience training without machines: "people always looking at me like, 'What the hell is this
guy doing?'" He traces the resistance partly to a purpose-disconnection built into conventional
fitness: **"When you look at like traditional functional fitness, it's like I'm deadlifting... Why?
I'm deadlifting to get stronger. It's never I'm deadlifting to be able to take something from point
A to point B."**
sections.heading: Why natural movement feels "odd," and conventional fitness's missing "why"

sections.body:
`[10:08]` For people unused to being outdoors, Gaspard starts indoors, working on the ground
"because they are not used to get up and sit down anymore" — calling MovNat's ground get-up
exercises "a really good addition" to the natural method. `[12:10]`–`[13:11]` For groups, the
natural method deliberately uses storytelling ("we have to face a danger, we have to pass through
an obstacle, we have to climb into a tree") to create a shared mood that gets participants
attempting movements without consciously deciding to: "they were not thinking they could do it, but
they just do it... they are just like, 'Whoa, what just happened?'"
sections.heading: Storytelling, group training, and get-ups as an entry point

sections.body:
`[14:12]`–`[15:12]` Asked for a favorite thing to teach, Gaspard names two "underestimated"
families: throwing and balancing. The interviewer extends the balance point with his own framing:
apparent simplicity ("stand on one leg... that's easy") gives way to real difficulty, and losing
balance is tied to losing focus on unrelated thoughts — "the next thing you know they're thinking
about the meeting they have to have at 3:00 and then they start to fall."
sections.heading: Favorite technique families: throwing and balancing

sections.body:
**The instructor's stated purpose in this session is not to teach the Turkish get-up as an
exercise, but to use it to demonstrate that tools and added load (a kettlebell, a 100 lb sandbag)
are teaching constraints that make a fundamental movement — standing up from lying down — more
learnable and efficient, not the source of the physical adaptation itself.** `[01:03]` "The tool
does not dictate the technique. The tool assist in the learning of the technique." `[36:39]` "I
want you to think of what is the movement, what's the problem you're trying to solve, and then
[use] a variety of constraints... Use the tool not as what's going to create the adaptation, but
what's going to help teach somebody."
sections.heading: Central claim

sections.body:
`[19:24]`–`[21:26]` The instructor frames all human movement as falling into domains: **manipulative**
("I manipulate my environment or myself around the environment... pick up something... point A to
point point B"), **locomotive** (getting from point A to point B without necessarily picking
anything up), **combative** (striking and grappling), and **expressive** ("I can move just because
I want to"). Get-up patterns are placed on the combative side of this map but are said to transfer
everywhere: "every get-up that you've ever seen in your life happens in grappling in some way or
another," citing the "shin box" stretch, "S-mount," and "octopus guard" as the same body positions
appearing in a different context.
sections.heading: The four domains of human movement

sections.body:
`[02:04]`–`[03:06]` The get-up is used specifically because "it teaches all the foundational
principles of human movement, which are tension and relaxation," and "how your points of support...
interact with the surface of support," with points of support diminishing (and stability
decreasing) as the body moves from lying down toward standing. The instructor teaches the sequence
in discrete named steps — body weight shift (rocking to the side), body weight transfer (onto
elbow, then hand), and the half-kneeling stand — coaching each student individually and adjusting
cues (e.g., "drive out of this foot," using momentum from a kicking leg) based on where each
student struggles.
sections.heading: Points of support, tension, and the teaching sequence

sections.body:
`[30:36]`–`[32:37]` Demonstrating with a 100 lb sandbag, the instructor shows that loading the
weight onto the hip/skeleton rather than letting it compress the torso makes an apparently harder
task easier, not harder: **"Once you get the... weight distribution... the technique... it's like
100 lb turning into 40."** The general principle stated: "as you load it, I'm always trying to make
sure that I'm loading my skeleton versus my tissue" — added intensity is reframed as a tool that
can reduce, not just increase, difficulty when applied correctly.
sections.heading: Loading and the "counter-balance" effect

sections.body:
None — this video is instructional/pedagogical, covering a movement pattern and teaching
philosophy rather than a symptom, injury, or health signal.
sections.heading: Symptoms and body signals addressed

sections.body:
- **Points of support** — the parts of the body in contact with the ground or another surface at a
  given moment; the get-up is taught partly to expose how these change and reduce in number as the
  body moves from lying to standing. `[02:04]`
- **Constraints-led approach** — using an object, template, or step-by-step breakdown ("scaffolding")
  to shape how a student solves a movement problem, rather than the object being the point of the
  exercise. `[07:10]`
- **Differential learning** — deliberately varying a movement slightly on each repetition (e.g.
  moving the hand position) to expose a learner to more variation rather than one fixed pattern.
  `[26:31]`
sections.heading: Glossary terms introduced

sections.body:
- The counter-balance framing: adding weight in the right place can make a movement *easier*, not
  harder — "100 lb turning into 40" once loaded correctly onto the hip/skeleton. `[32:37]`
- "There's so many different ways to skin a cat" — used to describe the many valid variations on
  solving the same movement problem (getting up off the floor). `[36:39]`
